highlights:

### A restore continues after you stop the node

You say to your agent

> “Wake my 80 GB node. If it is not ready in 15 minutes, stop it and try again later.”

If you stop a node while it restores from a snapshot, the next wake of the node now goes back to the same host if that host has room. The host keeps the downloaded parts that passed the checksum check for 6 hours, and the restore continues from those parts. On a different host, the download starts again from the beginning.

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

results.title: A Primer on Compute Markets
results.author: Morning Mist
highlights:
1. There is no price of compute. The same H100 rents for ~$1.95/hr on marketplaces and $8-9/hr at hyperscalers. An Itô Markets’ quote harvester pulled 1,417 quotes in a single day across 120 SKU-region-term combinations and found material same-day dispersion for identical silicon. Different configurations.
2. High volatility, zero hedging tools. Hourly rates can swing 137% in a year. Any other commodity this volatile has had a futures curve for a century.
3. A $1.5 trillion financing hole. Global data center spend is estimated at ~$3T through 2028, with $1.5T needed beyond hyperscaler cash flows. Lenders want contracted revenue, buyers won’t commit to years 4-5. The unfinanceable tail of a datacenter loan, months 30-60, is the single clearest product gap in the market.
4. The buyer base is exploding. It used to be five labs. Now it’s all companies that want to own models (Ramp, Harvey, Cursor, Airbnb running on Qwen), and there’s no one servicing the smaller guys.

...

- Indices: Silicon Data’s SDH100RT (H100 rental, live on Bloomberg since May 2025, ~3.5M data points/day, DRW-backed) plus a 1–36 month forward curve; Ornn’s OCPI (H100 printed $2.93 on Aug 28); SemiAnalysis’s contract-price index; Compute Desk’s indexes on 350k Bloomberg terminals. There is already a live term structure, and it’s in backwardation (H100 spot ~$2.72 vs ~$2.38 36-month), pricing in supply growth and chip succession exactly like an oil curve prices in balances.
- Futures: CME lists cash-settled H100 and B200 monthly rental futures on NYMEX October 5, 2026, pending regulatory review (settling on Silicon Data). ICE announced its own GPU futures on Ornn’s index. Architect, is going for perps on GPU and DRAM prices plus an exchange-for-physical bridge so futures can convert into actual delivered capacity. Three exchange groups announced listings for the same new commodity within three weeks of each other this May.
- Spot venues: SF Compute runs an order-book market where compute contracts are resellable. Compute Exchange runs auctions across 100+ providers and opened a used-GPU secondary market in July.
- Speculators and desks: Kalshi’s GPU markets did ~15x Polymarket’s volume and published a market-implied forward curve; Hyperliquid already trades H100 perps; Goldman and JPMorgan are exploring GPU futures desks. Itô Markets is building the agentic OTC desk layer.
- Credit: >$20B of GPU-collateralized loans outstanding, from CoreWeave’s facilities down to onchain:

...

- SF Compute: build data centers, and have an order-book spot market where compute contracts are resellable. ($40M Series A, DCVC, Wing)
- Compute Exchange: Marketplace for compute from neoclouds and others. Reserved-capacity auctions (1-36 months). (funding undisclosed, co-founded by DRW founder Don Wilson)
- Stoa: A gated venue discovering clearing levels for enterprise GPU hardware itself, financializing the box, not just the hour. ($500K, Y Combinator S26)
- RunPod and Vast: Airbnb-of-GPUs spot marketplaces. Spot prices, you can be evicted mid-run, but get it as sport. (RunPod: $20M seed, Intel Capital, Dell Technologies Capital; Vast: no disclosed VC)
- Computable: buy, sell and redeem dedicated H100 nodes by the calendar week, sealed-bid auctions, posted sell-back quotes, forward weeks priced into 2027, plus an open-source GPU price index. Built by ex-Jump Trading and Citadel Securities market-microstructure people. (YC 2026 batch)

highlights:
A daily record of what secure on-demand cloud GPUs cost per GPU-hour, computed from the current offers GPUPerHour tracks across cloud GPU providers. Published as a table and as CSV; no charts yet.

## What this index measures

Every day at 00:05 UTC the index records, for each of the 13 GPUs in the basket, the minimum, median and maximum price per GPU-hour across every current offer on the site. An offer is current only when all of the following hold:

- the provider reports it as available right now;
- the provider has live stock tracking, so "available" is a real-time observation, not a catalog entry;
- it was seen within the last 15 minutes;
- it is secure on-demand pricing on provider-operated data-center hardware, billed per GPU-hour;
- spot, interruptible, reserved and peer-to-peer or marketplace listings are excluded.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Halve to $3.43/Hr in 2026
results.author: Dr. Elena Marchetti
highlights:
Renting an Nvidia H100 for an hour costs anywhere from $1.30 an hour to as much as $12.29 in October 2026 according to Coloprice, depending on who you ask and which cloud you pick, with GPUFinder naming Lium as the cheapest confirmed H100 at $1.79 an hour and GPU marketplace tracker Uvik putting the median H100 SXM on-demand price at $4.20 across 16 surveyed providers on October 7. That spread, once a rounding error in a niche market, has become one of the clearest signals of how tight the AI compute supply chain still is, two years after ChatGPT turned GPU capacity into a boardroom talking point. Pricing trackers, bank analysts, and Nvidia’s own executives are now telling three overlapping stories at once: H100 rental costs have fallen by roughly half since early 2024, newer chips like the H200 and B200 command a steep premium, and the entire market remains bottlenecked by memory, not by silicon.

...

Pricing tracker Thunder Compute, in a blog post on H100 pricing dated September 1, 2026, lists on-demand H100 80GB rates spanning from $2.89 an hour on RunPod up to $10.98 an hour on Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g instances. CloudZero’s own H100 cost breakdown, published in late August 2026, puts the low end at Vast.ai for as little as $1.49 an hour, though GPUFinder’s October 2026 listing of $1.29 an hour on Hyperbolic now sets the floor, while Rank.ai listed Azure H100 capacity at $6.98 to $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, which stretches the spread at the top even wider. Between those two data points sits a real number that infrastructure teams have to budget against every quarter.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io
highlights:
337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

Published September 9, 2026 · Flopper.io Research

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

...

No two providers quote the same way. One prices an eight-GPU node, another a single accelerator, a third a monthly contract, and Scaleway prices in euros. Every listing goes through the same four steps before it reaches a page.

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

...

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

...

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

results.title: Why H100 Rental Prices Rose 40% While Token Prices Fell
results.author: Framesta Fernando
highlights:
> TL;DR: H100 rental prices rose almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour on one-year contracts, while API token prices kept falling. The cost floor under inference is rising even as the sticker price above it drops, and every self-hosting business case written before that shift is now wrong.

...

The number worth reading is the rental contract. H100 one-year rental pricing rose from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, close to 40%, and on-demand capacity was described as sold out across all GPU types, with half the providers surveyed unable to quote even 8 nodes of H100s or H200s (SemiAnalysis's H100 rental price index). That is not a market pricing in abundance. That is a market rationing.

...

### Q: How much does an H100 cost to rent per hour?

Published index pricing for one-year H100 contracts was $2.35 per GPU-hour as of March 2026, up from a $1.70 low in October 2025. On-demand and short-term rates sit higher and vary widely by provider and region, and during the 2026 crunch several providers could not quote capacity at any advertised rate. Treat a quoted rate as valid only for the term you can actually sign.

results.title: Starving for Compute: Price Targets Are Opinions — the H100 Rent Is the Fact
results.author: Victor Hale
highlights:
- Piper Sandler PIPR-- upgraded Nvidia/Broadcom as AI compute demand outpaces supply, citing a 30% rise in H100 GPU hourly rents to $2.60.

...

On Thursday, Piper Sandler PIPR-- started covering seven chipmakers and called the AI market "starving for more compute capacity." Overweight on Nvidia NVDA--, Broadcom AVGO--, AMD AMD--, Arm ARM--, and Marvell; Neutral on Intel INTC-- and Qualcomm; top picks on Nvidia and Broadcom. Analyst ratings and price targets are opinions, so I tend to look past them. But this particular note carried one operating detail worth stopping on: a four-year-old GPU, the H100, is now renting for $2.60 an hour, up from $2.00 in December.

...

Most of that is projection. What is not projection is the H100 rent. The H100 shipped in volume in late 2022. Nearly four years later, on a training-era chip that the market was supposed to have moved past, the spot price has gone up 30%, not down. Hardware that is supposed to be obsoleted does not get more expensive. That is the testable claim behind the thesis: scarcity is real enough that even last generation's silicon carries a premium, because demand for compute now exceeds how fast it can be manufactured and delivered for both training and inference.
